summary: Presents techniques for computing the Internet checksum efficiently in hardware. It includes programmable logic code for a single low-cost part that can do the work at high speed. It is informational.

eli5.summary: The checksum is a quick math check that your data did not get scrambled. This shows how to build a tiny chip that does that check very fast.

questions: how to implement internet checksum in hardware
how is the internet checksum calculated quickly
how does the internet checksum work
how to speed up checksum computation
subtitle: Efficient hardware implementation of the Internet Checksum at gigabit speeds

tldr.problem: As DMA (direct memory access) hardware began computing checksums during data transfers, implementing the Internet Checksum efficiently in software no longer worked. A dedicated hardware design was needed to perform checksumming without becoming a bottleneck.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC presents a pipelined, ones-complement adder design implemented in a low-cost programmable logic device (PLD). The design accumulates partial checksums over the high and low 16-bit halves of 32-bit data words in parallel, using carry-lookahead techniques to minimize latency.
tldr.outcome: The design achieves 1.26 Gbps throughput at 26 nanoseconds per 32-bit word, suitable for inclusion in PC host interface cards and DMA controllers, making hardware checksum computation practical and affordable.

today: RFC 1936 is Informational and describes hardware acceleration techniques for the Internet Checksum. The design and PLD implementation were relevant for 1990s-era systems. Modern CPUs have built-in checksum offloading capabilities and gigabit-speed operations, superseding the need for standalone PLD implementations.

sections.title: Hardware Acceleration of the Checksum
sections.content:
RFC 1936 addresses the implementation of the Internet Checksum in hardware. The checksum is computed over IP headers, UDP packets, TCP packets, and other protocol headers to detect corruption. Earlier RFCs showed how to compute it efficiently in software, often embedded in data copying operations.

With the rise of DMA hardware (which copies memory without CPU involvement), checksum computation moved into DMA controllers. Software-based checksumming of copied data became a bottleneck. The RFC authors designed a hardware implementation suitable for incorporation into a DMA engine, using an inexpensive programmable logic device (PLD) costing about 40 dollars in 1995.

This design has been implemented in the PC-ATOMIC host interface hardware and can sustain 1.26 Gbps transfer rates, processing one 32-bit word every 26 nanoseconds.
sections.eli5: Computers copy data around using special hardware. That hardware can also check if the data is correct, but only if the checking is super fast. This RFC shows how to make it that fast.

sections.title: Internet Checksum Fundamentals
sections.content:
The Internet Checksum is a simple but effective error detection code. It is computed as the complement (bitwise NOT) of the ones-complement sum of the data taken in 16-bit units. When you checksum the data and checksum together, you should get a result of all ones (a zero after inversion), indicating no errors.

The checksum has several useful properties: it is byte order independent, 16-bit word-order independent, and supports incremental computation. This means you can compute it in pieces and combine the results, or reorder data and recalculate without changing the outcome (within reason).

A standard implementation sums 16-bit halves one at a time. This RFC's approach computes two partial checksums in parallel: one for the high (odd) 16-bit half-words of the 32-bit data and one for the low (even) half-words. The two partial results are then combined with ones-complement addition and inverted to produce the final checksum.
sections.eli5: The checksum adds up numbers from your data. This design adds two batches of numbers at the same time, which is twice as fast.

sections.title: Ones-Complement Adder Design
sections.content:
The core of the design is a ones-complement lookahead adder. Unlike two's-complement addition (standard in most processors), ones-complement addition has a wrap-around carry that must return to the least significant bit position, creating a toroidal carry-lookahead structure.

Building a ones-complement adder from two's-complement components requires two adders or two cycles per addition. The RFC's design uses a native ones-complement lookahead adder, where all bits have the same complexity (that of the highest bit of a two's-complement adder). This makes the circuit uniform and pipelined.

The hardware implementation uses 2-bit and 3-bit full-lookahead sub-components chained in a ring via carry bit registers. This deferred carry propagation creates a pipeline: fast adder stages process data, and carries are stored in registers to be processed in the next cycle. On a PLD with 16 product terms, 3-bit components are the maximum, and the carries take at most 5 idle clock cycles to propagate through the pipeline.
sections.eli5: The adder is built like a ring of small adding machines. Each one adds a few bits, passes any leftover (the carry) to a register, and the next one processes it next cycle. This works like an assembly line.

sections.title: Hardware and Software Interfaces
sections.content:
The Internet Checksum device appears to software as a single 32-bit memory-mapped register. The register holds two 16-bit ones-complement sums (high and low half-words). Control signals handle clearing, output enable, clock cycling, input data latching, and addition triggering.

The CLK signal cycles the pipeline. The ICLK signal latches input data from the bus. The ADD signal (often tied to ICLK) causes the latched data to be accumulated into the checksum register. One 32-bit value can be latched and accumulated every 26 nanoseconds.

The final checksum is computed by folding the two halves: ones-complement adding the high and low 16-bit results together, then inverting the result. Software can clear the device, initiate transfers with checksumming enabled, and read the result when finished. The RFC provides detailed C code examples for initializing the device and extracting results.
sections.eli5: The device looks like a fast calculator hooked to the computer's memory bus. You tell it to start, it checksums whatever data flows past, and you read the final answer when done.
